name: AP Psychology
overview: AP Psychology introduces the scientific study of behavior and mental processes. The course was redesigned for 2024–25 around five units and four science practices, with a stronger emphasis on research methods, data interpretation, and applying concepts to scenarios. Free-response questions now ask students to analyze a research article and to build an argument from evidence.

sections.name: Section I
sections.notes: Many questions are set in scenarios or include data, graphs, or research summaries.

sections.name: Section II, Question 1
sections.notes: Analyze one research article summary: methods, variables, statistics, ethics, and generalizability.

sections.name: Section II, Question 2
sections.notes: Make a claim and support it with evidence from three provided sources and psychological concepts.

skills.name: Concept Application
skills.description: Apply psychological perspectives, theories, concepts, and research findings to a scenario.

skills.name: Research Methods and Design
skills.description: Identify and evaluate research methods, variables, sampling, and ethics.

skills.name: Data Interpretation
skills.description: Interpret quantitative data, including descriptive and inferential statistics, in tables and graphs.

skills.name: Argumentation
skills.description: Develop and justify a claim using evidence and psychological reasoning.

scoring.summary: Section I (75 MCQ) counts for two-thirds of the score and Section II (two 7-point FRQs) for one-third. The weighted composite is converted to a 1–5 score using cut points that change each year and are not published.

frqTypes.name: Article Analysis Question (AAQ)
frqTypes.howScored: One point each for tasks such as identifying the research method, operational definition of a variable, a statistic and its meaning, an ethical guideline followed, whether findings generalize, and how the findings support or refute a claim.

frqTypes.name: Evidence-Based Question (EBQ)
frqTypes.howScored: A defensible claim (1 point), then for two pieces of evidence from different sources: citing the evidence (1 point each) and explaining how it supports the claim using a psychological concept (2 points each).

strategy: Read every scenario for the concept being tested before reading answer choices; distractors are often real terms that don't fit the scenario.
Master research methods: experimental vs. correlational designs, operational definitions, random assignment vs. random sampling, and what each statistic tells you.
On the AAQ, answer exactly what each part asks in one or two precise sentences, using the article's details.
On the EBQ, cite sources by letter and explicitly link each piece of evidence to a named psychological concept.
Practice reading graphs and tables quickly: means, standard deviations, correlation coefficients, and effect sizes.
When two answers seem right, pick the one that matches the specific term in the stem (e.g., "best explains" vs. "best describes").
Budget about 70 seconds per multiple-choice question.
pitfalls: Confusing random sampling (generalizability) with random assignment (causal inference).
Mixing up negative reinforcement and punishment.
Confusing similar terms: sensation vs. perception, assimilation vs. accommodation, proactive vs. retroactive interference.
Defining a term on FRQs without applying it to the scenario.
Writing vague claims on the EBQ that can't be supported with the sources.
